units.translation: 49. "and he was eager": he was in desire; but now it stands for "he rushed upon and desired." The word also means "he groaned": "they groaned around the iron" (Iliad 23.30).
50. "to scatter": to disperse. Lg
51. Lycoreus: this man has been invented by the poet, not taken from history.
52-53a. "straps": the so-called "ants." "Dry" instead of "parched"; hence some say that Arcadia was called not after King Azan, but because Azania is rough; for it is rough and dry.
b. "and they were around": they were excessively emaciated. Hence also "leg" is the fleshless part of the body, and "scrawny man" from this.
54. "overweening": arrogant. The metaphor is from the phiale; for its overflow is "hyperphialon", meaning "excessive". A phiale is a kind of cauldron-shaped vessel.

55-56a. "without lot": apart from casting lots. And through this again he shows him arrogant. The phrase "so that you may not blame me afterwards" as if he already trusted victory to himself. And this is barbaric. For if the lot knows how to resolve strife
and to give equal things to each, how would he later be likely to contend against him? For rather now he would have quarreled if he had not been allotted.

b. "you may blame": so that you may not find fault with me later as having received inferior things. For the younger poets understood "atembesthai" not in the sense of "to be deprived", but in the sense of "to blame".
60. "in a challenging manner": provocatively. Lg (P)
62. "without excuse": without hesitation, without distinction, making no pretext for the killing. Lg P
64. "exhorting": instead of "urging on". Lg (P)
65. "they knew" is used for the plural "they knew", as also "of her there were three heads" (Hesiod, Theogony 321). P
66. "binding in evil fate": in evil destiny. Lg
67. "when they stood apart with straps": they prepared themselves at a distance from each other. Lg (P)
68a. "of the limbs": here, of the faces. Lg
b. "Rhethos" is every limb, but here the face. P

70-74a. "like a wave of the sea": just as, he says, a wave rising up strikes a ship, but by the skill of the helmsman who turns it aside the ship escapes, so also Amycus pressed upon him to frighten him, but he, avoiding him, was unwounded. L
b. "escapes": flees. Because of his roughness and his violent rush he likens Amycus to a wave, and Polydeuces to a skilled helmsman.
c. "terrifying": disturbing; by his dense rush against him he did not allow him to delay.
75-78a. "darting": the preposition "under" is missing, so that it is "darting under" and "fleeing from" Amycus by his own skill he remained unwounded and unharmed. L
b. "and quickly perceiving his ruthlessness": perceiving, he says, Polydeuces, where he was ineffective and easy to attack, engaged his hands with him, standing his ground.
